items.title: A new approach to observing intuition during crisis exercises: linguistic markers of cognitive heuristics
items.abstract: Organisations are using crisis exercises to train their crisis management staff. Few studies have examined intuitive decision-making during exercises, which manifests itself in the form of heuristics: cognitive shortcuts. Identifying these heuristics duringobservation of exercises is complex due to the lack of a methodology for considering heuristics during exercises. To overcome this problem, we propose a methodology for observing linguistic markers to identify heuristics during 32 crisis exercises at the French Alternative Energies and Atomic Energy Commission. This research has shown that our methodology provides a framework for identifying seven specific heuristics during crisis exercises. We conclude the article with the contributions of our methodology and prospects for further development.

items.title: A novel cloud-enabled enterprise information systems framework for accelerating digital transformation strategies
items.abstract: The co-evolution of micro-frontend UIs and backend microservices in cloud-native environments is complicated by UI–API semantic drift, dynamic workloads, and safe-deployment constraints. A tripartite agentic AI framework is introduced that combines reinforcement-learning (RL) agents for adaptive runtime control, large-language-model (LLM) synthesizers for automated artifact generation, and policy-as-code governors for security and compliance enforcement. The co-evolution process is formulated as a drift-aware Markov decision process, while Kubernetes-native traffic shifting supports progressive rollout and rollback. KubeSim was used for offline policy training; the reported performance results were obtained from live AWS EKS, Google GKE, and Azure AKS clusters. Across five benchmarks, the framework achieved a mean resolution success rate of 91.4%, compared with 62.0% for rule-based control, 71.1% for a controlled zero-shot LLM baseline, and 79.0% for partial RL. The framework also reduced normalized mean time to recovery by 80%, normalized change failure rate by 75%, and CPU utilization by 30 percentage points, while attaining a 98% audit pass rate. Component-removal and counterfactual-return analyses indicate complementary contributions from adaptive control, artifact synthesis, and policy enforcement. These results support the effectiveness, scalability, and governability of the framework for cloud-native enterprise digital transformation.

items.title: A Paradox Perspective
items.abstract: This chapter investigates how artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping medical professionalism, drawing on paradox theory, particularly the automation-augmentation paradox, to analyse how medical work is being redefined. While the medical profession has historically been able to balance resistance and adaptation to external pressures, AI represents a qualitatively different challenge: it encroaches on core professional expertise, introduces new knowledge agents into clinical decision-making, and disrupts traditional power structures between doctors, patients, and clinical knowledge. This chapter discusses how current AI deployments predominantly augment medical judgement, especially in specialties such as radiology, cardiology, and neurology. Yet the trajectory of AI integration suggests an evolving interplay between augmentation and automation, requiring clinicians to strategically engage with technologies that both complement and potentially transform their expertise. A central focus is on how AI might help address longstanding cognitive and implicit biases in medical decision-making related to race, gender, age, disability, and socioeconomic status. Although AI offers opportunities to reduce inequities, it also risks replicating or amplifying them due to biased training data, design choices, and opaque algorithms. This chapter argues for a hybrid model of medical doctor-AI collaboration that leverages mutual learning, preserves professional responsibility, and embeds safeguards to mitigate bias.

items.title: A PILOT STUDY TO EVALUATE DIFFERENCES IN SPINAL ANGLES DURING A SEATED COMPUTER TASK COMPARED WITH A SELF-SELECTED OPTIMAL SITTING POSTURE
items.abstract: Conflicts of interest: No conflicts of interest Sources of funding: No funding obtained Background Low back pain is the leading cause of years lived with disability worldwide and consequently it is the most common condition treated by physiotherapists in an out-patient setting. Physiotherapists also have a role to play in preventing spinal pain by providing ergonomic education. Purpose of Study To compare spinal angles whilst conducting a seated typing task with a self-selected optimal posture. Methods Cross-sectional pilot study. Twenty asymptomatic participants (9 male, 11 female, aged 19 to 23 years) adopted their normal sitting working posture using a laptop to conduct a typing task; they were then asked to adopt what they considered to be their best sitting posture. Retroreflective markers were attached to: L4, ASIS, PSIS, T12, C7, tragus and canthus. Spinal (neck, thoracic, lumbar and pelvic) angles were established via digital photographs using a bespoke MATLAB programme (MathWorks). Statistical analysis (Wilcoxon signed ranks tests) was conducted to determine between condition differences. Results No statistically significant results were observed between conditions for pelvic angles (p>0.05), however statistically significant differences (p<0.05) were observed for lumbar, thoracic and neck angles. In all cases participants adopted more ‘upright’ optimal postures. Conclusion The results suggest that a self-selected optimal posture varies significantly with a computer working posture for lumbar, thoracic and neck angles. Whilst pelvic angles were not significantly different between conditions, descriptive analysis demonstrated a more flexed position for all angles during the working posture. Whilst an optimal posture remains debatable, these differences highlight the need to identify interventions to address differences between working and optimal postures.

items.title: A Proposed Model for Teachers' AI Competencies Based on UNESCO and DigCompEdu Frameworks: A Qualitative Study
items.abstract: Teachers’ competencies in artificial intelligence (AI) constitute a fundamental element for achieving innovative and effective education aligned with the demands of the twenty-first century. This study aims to propose a comprehensive model of teachers’ AI competencies based on the UNESCO AI Competency Framework for Teachers and the European Digital Competence Framework for Educators (DigCompEdu), while adapting them to suit the needs of teacher preparation programs in faculties of education. The study adopts a qualitative approach using focus groups with experts in curriculum and instruction as well as educational technology. The domains, standards, and indicators of both frameworks were analyzed and discussed in order to derive a practical and contextually relevant model. The study resulted in a proposed model comprising five main domains, 15 standards, and 48 performance indicators, covering cognitive, pedagogical, ethical, professional, and assessment dimensions. It also provides practical recommendations for developing teacher preparation and continuous professional development programs, with a focus on integrating artificial intelligence in a responsible and effective manner to support interactive and inclusive learning for students.

items.title: A Return to Natural Human Learning in the Age of AI: Active Agency, Applied Curiosity and a Human-Governed Architecture for Augmented Understanding
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is frequently described as if increasing computational capability were equivalent to increasing intelligence. This article rejects that scalar assumption and repositions artificial systems within a broader account of Natural Human Learning. It synthesises the 2026 Benjamin et al. work on cCC*, agency, bounded choice, Socialwork*, AEIOUF and consciousing; the Benjamin-McLaughlin account of Applied Curiosity and Augmented Understanding; the Benjamin-Palmer development of W-ALL as an externalised, revisable learning field; and the Natural Learning triptych's account of embodied, pre-verbal and AI-age learning. The synthesis is named LUMO: a human-governed learning environment in which machine generation enlarges the field of chances without displacing human authorship of choices, changes, responsibility or meaning. The paper advances four connected claims. First, learning begins before artificial representation - and before language: natural processes, embodiment, neural dynamics, encounter and difference provide the "horse" before the computational "cart". Second, uniquely human active agency (AAA) is categorical rather than scalar: capability may increase, but agency is not made "super" by more computation. Third, cCC* (Curiosity → Chances → Choices → Changes) is operationalised through the sequential AEIOUF process, A → E → I → O → U → F, with Conative Situational Integration (CSI) maintaining continuity across transitions. Fourth, LUMO should be coupled to protected canonical infrastructure: LUMO supports porous exploration; LIMO, with PROTON guardrails, protects provenance, permissions, canonical state and authorised change. R1-R16 and the 96-facet R × AEIOUF address space provide a selective-context routing layer, while CQI and CGI distinguish inquiry from generative construction. In the age of AI, the binding criterion becomes the preservation of the learner's CAN before externally supplied COULD. The resulting architecture reframes AI as a contingent support to human Natural Learning rather than its model, endpoint or successor. Sixteen research propositions are specified for empirical evaluation.

items.title: A Situation Monitoring, Analysis, and Reporting Team (SMART) framework for structuring Situational Awareness (SA) in construction projects
items.abstract: Construction projects are socio-technical systems requiring shared Situation Awareness (SA) to manage uncertainty and change. This study proposes Situation Monitoring, Analysis, and Reporting Teams (SMART) as a human-centred framework for structuring shared SA in construction. A thematic literature review identified a gap in understanding SA as an ongoing socio-technical process. An exploratory pilot study in a simulated modular construction setting examines communication patterns across four reporting phases: no reporting, self-reporting, SMART reporting, and post-intervention. SMART reporting was associated with a shift from fragmented to more structured and task-oriented communication, alongside increased information sharing and task-related exchanges. These patterns indicate coordination and information exchange, not direct measures of SA. The study makes three contributions: (1) reconceptualizing SA as an organizational socio-technical process rather than an individual or technology-driven outcome; (2) introducing SMART as a mechanism linking monitoring, sensemaking, and reporting; and (3) providing exploratory evidence that structured reporting is associated with communication patterns linked to SA processes. The controlled pilot setting and use of proxy indicators bounds findings. Future research should test SMART in real-world scenarios and examine its integration with digital and AI-assisted tools.

items.title: A socio-computational framework for evaluating artificial intelligence adoption readiness in small-scale businesses
items.abstract: Purpose Adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) across small-scale businesses remains uneven even with the growing pace of digital transformation. Large enterprises are rapidly integrating AI into their operations, while there is still a barrier to adoption within small-scale businesses. This study proposes and examines an exploratory computational readiness index (CRI) that brings together behavioral, organizational and environmental dimensions to understand the preparedness of small-scale businesses in adopting AI. This index is offered as a preliminary firm-level diagnostic rather than a fully validated measure. Design/methodology/approach A quantitative, multi-source design was used, combining primary survey data from small-scale businesses with secondary global data collected from international sources and informal conversations with additional small business owners, managers and employees who fell outside the formal survey sample. Survey instruments were used to capture behavioral, organizational and environmental factors influencing the decision to adopt AI. This was also complemented with secondary global data collected and combined to derive the readiness index. Appropriate statistical tests were conducted to examine relationships among key dimensions and the overall readiness index. Findings Organizational factors like employee skills, motivation and opportunities were most consistently linked with readiness across groups, followed by individuals’ behavioral factors. External factors such as infrastructure and environment appeared to have comparatively smaller influence. The results of the study have been used to develop a readiness index that is intended to indicate the extent to which a small-scale business may be prepared to adopt AI. Practical implications The CRI proposed in this study can become a practical tool for policymakers and leaders within small-scale businesses for readiness assessment, prioritizing capability building within the organization rather than focusing on infrastructure investments alone. Originality/value This study contributes to the literature by proposing a novel framework for assessing AI readiness in small-scale businesses, integrating human, organizational and environmental dimensions.

items.title: A Standardized Benchmarking Framework for the Automated Evaluation of AI-Generated Travel Plans
items.abstract: The rapid adoption of large language models (LLMs) transformed the way users obtained travel recommendations and generated personalized travel plans. However, standardized methods for comparing AI-generated travel itineraries across heterogeneous providers remained limited. This study presented the design, implementation, and experimental evaluation of a web-based benchmarking framework for the standardized and automated comparison of AI-generated travel plans. The framework integrated standardized prompt generation, structured JSON response processing, field-level comparison, deterministic rule-based scoring, model ranking, and exportable benchmarking reports. It was evaluated across three travel-planning scenarios involving Prague, Rome, and Tokyo, with three independent benchmark executions attempted for each scenario, resulting in 27 provider-level requests. Eight executions produced complete three-provider comparisons; one Rome execution was incomplete because Microsoft Phi returned malformed JSON. Across the eight complete executions, Gemini achieved a mean structural-completeness score of 57.00/57 (SD = 0.00), ChatGPT achieved 47.38/57 (SD = 3.02), and Microsoft Phi achieved 34.63/57 (SD = 5.26), with the same rank ordering observed in all complete comparisons. Supplementary constraint-compliance analysis demonstrated that structural completeness did not necessarily imply full satisfaction of travel requirements. Sustainability-related outputs were additionally examined as a separate dimension. The results demonstrated consistent framework operation under the tested scenarios and repetitions while emphasizing the need to distinguish structural completeness from constraint compliance, factual accuracy, practical feasibility, and sustainability-related performance.

items.title: A Study on the Adoption and Responsible Use of Generative AI Tools for Sustainable Learning among Undergraduate Students
items.abstract: Abstract Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) has emerged as a transformative technology in higher education, significantly influencing the way students learn, access information, complete academic tasks, and develop professional skills. Tools such as ChatGPT, Google Gemini, Microsoft Copilot, and Canva AI have become increasingly popular among commerce students for assignments, presentations, exam preparation, and concept clarification. While these technologies offer opportunities for personalized and efficient learning, their growing use also raises concerns regarding academic integrity, ethical practices, critical thinking, and dependency on AI-generated content. This study aims to examine the adoption and responsible use of Generative AI tools among commerce students in higher education and to evaluate their contribution towards sustainable learning. The research adopts a descriptive and analytical research design using primary data collected through a structured questionnaire administered to commerce students. The study focuses on students' awareness of GenAI tools, frequency and purpose of usage, responsible AI practices, AI dependency, and the perceived impact of AI on academic productivity and sustainable learning outcomes. The study is expected to provide insights into how commerce students integrate Generative AI into their academic learning and whether they use these tools responsibly by verifying information, avoiding plagiarism, and using AI as a learning aid rather than a substitute for independent thinking. It also explores the relationship between AI adoption, ethical usage, and sustainable learning practices in the context of higher education. The findings of this research are expected to assist educators, higher education institutions, and policymakers in designing AI literacy initiatives, promoting responsible AI usage, and developing pedagogical practices aligned with the objectives of sustainable and inclusive education. The study contributes to the growing body of literature on Artificial Intelligence in commerce education by emphasizing the importance of balancing technological innovation with ethical responsibility and lifelong learning in higher education. Keywords: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI), Responsible AI, Sustainable Learning, Commerce Students, Higher Education, AI Ethics, Academic Productivity, Digital Literacy.

items.title: A Systematic Review of Data Mining Frameworks and AIEnabled Neural Network Technologies for Environmentally Sustainable Indian Agriculture: Trends, Challenges, and Future Directions
items.abstract: Agriculture remains the backbone of the Indian economy, contributing significantly to food security, employment, and rural development. However, increasing climate variability, soil degradation, water scarcity, pest infestations, fragmented landholdings, and the growing demand for sustainable food production have created substantial challenges for conventional farming practices. The rapid advancement of Data Mining, Artificial Intelligence (AI), Machine Learning (ML), and Deep Learning (DL) technologies has transformed precision agriculture by enabling intelligent analysis of large-scale agricultural data and supporting evidence-based decision-making. This systematic review critically examines recent developments in Data Mining frameworks and AI-enabled neural network technologies for environmentally sustainable Indian agriculture. The review synthesizes contemporary research on data acquisition, preprocessing, feature engineering, classification, clustering, association rule mining, regression analysis, and predictive analytics, together with advanced neural network architectures such as Artificial Neural Networks (ANN), Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN), Recurrent Neural Networks (RNN), Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), Gated Recurrent Units (GRU), Transformer models, and Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) [2], [3], [15], [18], [20], [21], [22], [43]. Furthermore, it evaluates their applications in crop yield prediction, soil health monitoring, intelligent irrigation, crop disease detection, weather forecasting, precision nutrient management, climate-resilient farming, and environmental sustainability [5], [11], [16], [24], [30], [36], [37]. The review identifies current research trends, methodological limitations, implementation challenges, and emerging opportunities while highlighting the need for scalable, interpretable, and resourceefficient intelligent agricultural systems tailored to India's diverse agro-climatic conditions. Finally, future research directions are proposed, emphasizing hybrid AI frameworks, Explainable AI, Edge Intelligence, Federated Learning, multimodal data integration, and sustainable decision-support systems. The findings provide a comprehensive knowledge base for researchers, policymakers, and agricultural practitioners seeking to develop intelligent, environmentally responsible, and sustainable agricultural ecosystems.

items.title: A Systems Engineering Design Framework for University Air Traffic Control Simulators: Integrating Regulatory Requirements, Human Factors, and Infrastructure Design
items.abstract: Air traffic control (ATC) simulators are essential tools for controller training, operational research and higher education, enabling realistic practice without affecting live air traffic. Although commercial simulation platforms are widely available, limited research has addressed structured engineering methodologies for designing university-based ATC simulation facilities that integrate regulatory, ergonomic, and technical requirements. This paper proposes a systems engineering framework for the conceptual design of university ATC simulators, combining stakeholder requirements, international aviation regulations, human factors principles, and engineering design within a requirement-driven workflow. The framework supports the design process from requirements analysis and functional decomposition to architectural layout, visualization system design, and technical infrastructure planning. Its applicability is demonstrated through the conceptual development of a 360° panoramic ATC simulator for higher education, comprising a 6.90 m diameter cylindrical screen driven by eight synchronized 4K laser projectors (effective horizontal resolution 19,968 pixels, 1.08 arcmin/pixel), a total usable floor area of approximately 278 m2, and an estimated installed electrical power of 25 kW. Furthermore, the framework incorporates universal design principles and specialized accessibility guidelines to ensure full ergonomic and physical accommodation for students with special needs. The proposed solution integrates the main functional areas of the simulation facility, including visualization, operator workstations, communication systems, and supporting infrastructure, while ensuring compliance with relevant standards and educational requirements. The proposed framework provides a structured and reusable methodology for the development of university ATC simulators and can support future educational and research simulation projects by improving design consistency, traceability, and scalability.

items.title: Accuracy of transfer learning in predicting peri-implantitis onset from intraoral radiograph: A multi-center longitudinal retrospective study
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: The growing application of artificial intelligence in dentistry has opened new opportunities for predicting peri-implantitis (PI) using convolutional neural networks (CNNs). Transfer learning, where knowledge from a model pre-trained on a large dataset is adapted to a new, domain-specific task, may enhance performance, particularly when medical datasets are limited. This study evaluated the ability of several pre-trained CNN architectures applied to baseline 2D intraoral radiographs to predict peri-implantitis onset. METHODS: A retrospective multi-center study was conducted at the University of Michigan and King's College London. A total of 195 implants (146 from Michigan and 49 from London) placed in 108 maintained patients were included. For each implant, a baseline periapical radiograph taken up to one year after prosthetic restoration was analyzed. Five pre-trained CNN architectures (ResNet50, DenseNet, VGG16, InceptionV3, EfficientNet) were combined with four transfer learning strategies: feature extraction (hybrid and non-hybrid), partial fine-tuning (50% of layers), and full fine-tuning. Models were trained using patient-wise splits to avoid leakage, and performance was evaluated on an independent test set using accuracy, area under the ROC curve (AUC), sensitivity, and specificity. RESULTS: All CNN architectures showed variable performance across transfer learning strategies. The non-hybrid feature extraction approach provided the most consistent discrimination, with the best models achieving AUC values between 0.74 and 0.83. InceptionV3 reached the highest AUC (0.83). Fine-tuning strategies yielded modest or low performance, with AUCs generally ranging from 0.42 to 0.69 across architectures. CONCLUSION: Non-hybrid feature extraction applied to pre-trained CNNs showed the most promising, though moderate, performance for predicting PI onset from baseline intraoral radiographs. These findings indicate that transfer learning may assist early risk stratification in implant dentistry, but larger prospective studies are needed before clinical adoption. CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Deep learning models may serve as adjunctive tools to identify implants at higher risk for future PI based on routine baseline radiographs, supporting more individualized maintenance protocols and earlier preventive interventions.

items.title: Action-oriented Narratives. How Innovation Emerges from Crowd Discussions
items.abstract: Crowds are increasingly invited to tackle complex innovation problems. However, our understanding of how crowds solve these problems has limited our ability to utilize them effectively. In this article, we examine how a crowd tasked with finding ways to preserve New Zealand’s native flora and fauna achieves solutions to this complex innovation problem through discussion. Our analysis reveals that discussions leading to innovative solutions differ from those leading to non-innovative solutions: innovation-yielding discussions (1) mobilize more Resources than Constraints, (2) converge on a single Goal, and (3) specify few (often one) responsible Subject(s); vis-à-vis, discussions leading to non-innovative solutions often surfaced multiple goals—thereby sustaining multiple problem framings—while subjects remained vague, implicit, or multiplied, and constraints frequently outnumbered resources. Moreover, we show how the specific weavings of these discursive elements support the crowd’s navigation of the complex innovation problem. Three discursive maneuvers – subject-goal anchoring, repurposing distant knowledge, and layering resources – are fundamental navigational tools used by the crowd to form what we call ‘action-oriented narratives:’ simple, dynamic, and evolving linguistic structures that enable collective problem exploration while giving room for localized improvisation. We contribute to the literature on problem solving by showing how specific linguistic activities alter individuals’ capacity to contribute to and solve complex problems. We also contribute to the literature on linguistic structures supporting innovation by showing that the types of discussions that support innovation depend on the openness of the setting.

items.title: Adapting Vision Foundation Models with Synthetic Data for Open-Pit Mining Crack Segmentation
items.abstract: Automatic crack segmentation in open-pit mining is constrained by the scarcity of representative, labeled datasets. Vision foundation models (VFMs) offer transferable visual representations, but their training-free performance on mining imagery and the benefits of synthetic-only adaptation remain insufficiently established. This study evaluates training-free VFM pipelines and investigates whether synthetic supervision improves their transfer to real-world crack imagery. SynthMineCrack is introduced as a diverse open-pit mining crack dataset, supporting model training and hyperparameter selection without real imagery or manual annotations. SAM 3 is adapted using low-rank adaptation (LoRA), layer normalization (LN) tuning, and adapters, individually and jointly, and compared with task-specific models trained on the same synthetic data. Evaluation on both in- and out-of-domain datasets shows that SAM 3 achieves the strongest training-free performance, while joint adaptation of all three operators improves intersection-over-union (IoU) on the mining evaluation dataset by 18.25 percentage points (pp). This configuration achieves a mean IoU of 69.39% across the five datasets, exceeding SegFormer, the strongest task-specific model, by 10.77 pp. Diagnostic analyses associate these gains with more complete crack recovery while the pretrained visual representation remains largely preserved. This configuration updates only 0.326% of the instantiated model’s parameter count and incurs little additional inference overhead. Together, these findings support synthetic-only adaptation as a practical means of improving SAM 3 for real-world crack segmentation while retaining inference requirements close to those of the base model.

items.title: Adaptive Leadership for Innovation: Exploring School Principals' Roles in AI-driven Educational Reform in Hong Kong
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly influencing various sectors of society, and education is at the forefront of this transformation. These emerging technologies are reshaping how students interact with content and how teachers design instruction, which create an urgent need for innovation. The success of such innovation in schools often depends on leadership that is flexible and adaptive to diverse cultural, technological, and organizational contexts. Drawing on the case of Hong Kong, this study investigated how school leaders perceive educational innovation in an AI-driven era and how they enact their leadership to engage teachers in these initiatives. Findings show that leaders recognize the multifaceted challenges of AI integration and use adaptive leadership to address them by prioritizing adaptive challenges, mobilizing teachers, and empowering them to experiment and change. The study contributes empirical evidence on adaptive leadership in AI-driven education and recommends practical strategies for engaging teachers in innovation. Its implications extend beyond Hong Kong and provide valuable guidance for school systems worldwide as they navigate ongoing innovation and build the capacity to meet future challenges.

items.title: Advancing clinical integration in undergraduate dental education through AI-enabled instructional design: a qualitative thematic analysis
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Despite growing interest in artificial intelligence (AI) in health professions education, qualitative evidence for integarting AI-supported instructional redesign on teaching practices and students' experiences in undergraduate dental education remains limited. The aim of this study was to explore the educational impact of AI-supported instructional redesign of lessons in undergraduate dental education. METHODS: We conducted this inductive qualitative thematic analysis in an undergraduate dental education setting. Existing lessons were redesigned using AI-supported recommendations to strengthen alignment between learning objectives, authentic clinical contexts, and expected clinical outcomes. Data were collected through classroom observations and students' focus group discussions. An inductive thematic analysis was performed, and findings from multiple data sources were curated, collecetd, and triangulated to enhance credibility. RESULTS: AI-supported instructional redesign transformed teaching by promoting authentic clinical scenarios, clinically oriented discussions, and explicit reasoning activities. Thematic analysis identified four interconnected themes: (1) a shift from teacher-centred knowledge delivery to facilitation of clinical reasoning; (2) transformation from passive attendance to active cognitive engagement; (3) building clinical meaning through authentic clinical contexts and collaborative dialogue; and (4) creating conditions for professional learning through psychological safety. AI functioned as a pedagogical design-support tool rather than replacing the educators' instructional role. Overall, the observed educational changes appeared to arise primarily from the pedagogical redesign enabled by AI-supported planning rather than from students' direct interaction with AI. CONCLUSION: This study endorses the role of AI-supported instructional redesign in enriching the existing undergraduate dental curriculum. This approach can potentially help educators align learning objectives, instructional strategies, and authentic clinical contexts. The reported educational modifications reflect primarily the implementation of learner-centred and clinically oriented pedagogical strategies, with AI functioning as a design-support mechanism rather than as a direct instructional agent.

items.title: Advancing Regional NO2 Estimation Using Machine Learning, TEMPO Satellite Data, and Geospatial Embeddings
items.abstract: Abstract Ground-level air quality affects human health, well-being, and social outcomes. Gold-standard monitoring relies on calibrated, ground-based sensors that can be costly to install and maintain, limiting spatial coverage especially in resource-constrained regions that face higher pollution burdens. Recent advances in satellite remote sensing and machine learning offer a pathway to address these limitations by extending the spatial and temporal coverage of monitoring networks. However, models trained at national or global scales often exhibit substantial variability in regional performance, particularly in environments that are data-sparse or with heterogeneous emission sources. In this work, we investigate the benefits of developing a regional model for the American Gulf South. We develop an ensemble machine learning model that integrates satellite-derived NO2 retrievals with auxiliary data sets, including pretrained AlphaEarth location embeddings, to incorporate globally learned spatial representations into a regional framework. We show that these embeddings improve model performance and enable the most detailed estimates to date: ∼1 km × 1 km estimates of daily maximum NO2 across the Gulf South. These results demonstrate how combining regional modeling approaches with global foundation model representations can improve air quality estimation in complex environments, providing new information to support exposure assessment and decision-making in under-monitored communities.

items.title: Adversarial Post-Training of Foundation Models for High-Frequency Trading
items.abstract: While autoregressive foundation models trained on limit order book (LOB) data show state-of-the-art performance for market simulation, pre-training with cross-entropy neither penalizes the compounding of sampling errors over free-running rollouts nor targets desired market properties. We introduce a post-training method for LOB foundation models using a Wasserstein generative adversarial network (GAN) objective. A critic, trained online on rollouts through the true, non-differentiable matching engine, guides updates from evolution strategies over rank-4 LoRA perturbations of the pre-trained generator, under a KL trust region. For efficiency, we use EGGROLL (Evolution Guided GeneRal Optimisation via Low-rank Learning), a memory-efficient variant of evolution strategies. On a held-out panel, adversarial post-training improves LOB-Bench realism by 17.6% (WS-21) and 17.0% (Mean-$L_1$), while selection-matched random-perturbation and compute-matched continued-pre-training controls yield no improvement. Post-training is thus a necessary stage that more pre-training does not replace. Per-position divergence measurements show that it slows error accumulation over 500-message rollouts from $3.1\times$ to $2.3\times$. Adversarial post-training is also inexpensive, requiring under 50M training tokens and 12 GPU-hours per seed, three orders of magnitude below the 48B-token pre-training budget. Ablations over critic inputs, optimizers, and the population-rollout trade-off, together with an analysis of reward hacking, yield practical design guidelines for adversarial post-training.

items.title: AfriGuard: Safety and Robust Refusal For African Languages
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) designed to interact with users are typically trained to respond appropriately to harmful or toxic content. However, ensuring appropriate responses becomes more challenging in diverse linguistic and cultural contexts, where safety risks may be expressed or interpreted differently. Building safe AI systems therefore requires detecting safety risks, understanding their nature, and responding appropriately, while accounting for linguistic and cultural variations that add complexity to each stage. In this work, we introduce AfriGuard, a culturally grounded multilingual dataset for studying harmful intent, safety-category understanding, and refusal behavior across 10 African languages and English. Our findings reveal that guardrail models underperform both open- and closed-source LLMs on safety-intent and safety-category classification, while models show limited understanding of appropriate safety behavior, scoring below 60% F1. We further find that models often fail to respond appropriately to unsafe prompts not because they explicitly refuse, but because they produce linguistically inadequate responses that result in incidental non-assistance rather than proper refusals. Finally, using AfriGuard, we develop efficient guardrail models that achieve performance competitive with models up to 30x larger, introduce refusal detectors that improve average performance by 43.9% over existing detectors, and demonstrate that supervised fine-tuning can substantially improve overall safety performance.

items.abstract: Agent-friendly Provenance Capture with con-duct Presenters Austin Macdonald , ORCID 0000-0002-8124-807X Cody C. Baker , ORCID 0000-0002-0829-4790 John A. Lee , ORCID 0000-0001-5884-4247 Yaroslav O. Halchenko , ORCID 0000-0003-3456-2493 All: Center for Open Neuroscience, Department of Psychological and Brain Sciences, Dartmouth College Keywords agentic workflows, provenance, reproducibility, resource monitoring, HPC Abstract Whether trying out a new tool, testing pipelines, or meticulously analyzing data for research, the daily work of RSEs and their agents depends on keeping context lean but relevant. The terminal outputs of tools and scripts frequently hold the necessary information, but they are often either bloating an agent’s context window, or forgotten after a human’s terminal scrolls past the buffer. con-duct is a lightweight, Python-based command line tool with no third-party dependencies: just use duct instead of to run a command. A wrapped run leaves a trail: full stdout and stderr streamed to disk (or skipped, for sensitive output); resource usage sampled across the command’s process tree; and a record of the invocation, wall clock time, peak memory, exit code, and system and environment details. Workflow managers and experiment trackers produce richer records (the poster compares them); con-duct collects basic provenance with so little effort it can be used on everything, producing uniform records. In daily work, humans and agents now execute commands side by side. Using con-duct, the full record stays out of the context window until it is needed. Even better, multiple runs can be filtered and grepped, ready for the questions nobody knew to ask. When did our tests start having that warning? Did this run take longer? con-duct ls makes the answers discoverable, filtering on any captured field with a Python expression: con-duct ls -e "message==' '" retrieves runs tagged at capture time with duct -m " ". con-duct ls -e "exit_code != 0" lists failures. con-duct ls -e "peak_rss > 8e9" finds runs that exceeded a memory budget. At the tool level, projects can adopt con-duct internally rather than reinventing per-tool monitoring: ReproNim’s containers [5] and ReproStim [6] both offer it already, and the same con-duct ls queries read their records. For research, the record stops being a convenience, and starts being a part of the provenance chain [4]. Pairing con-duct with datalad (git-based version control for data)[2] is an easy win for rigor. datalad run "duct ..." completes the execution and then commits the diff (including the duct logs). On HPC, last month’s measured wall time and peak memory are already recorded, and can help inform tomorrow’s SLURM request. When an expensive job fails, the bug-report evidence is already on disk, no re-run necessary to file an issue. con-duct is on PyPI (pip install con-duct), conda-forge, registered as RRID:SCR_025436, and developed openly [1]. The poster shows three real cases: an fMRIPrep run on a SLURM cluster, its five hours of CPU and memory plotted from the record; a Kubernetes upgrade worked deploy by deploy, with every attempt’s command, exit code, and wall time kept by con-duct; and duct wrapped around duct to measure its own overhead. Keeping agents’ work auditable will take more than one tool; con-duct is one small piece: a wrapper that makes the agent’s work, like the human’s, leave a trace. AI disclosure (per IEEE policy): Prose in the Abstract and Connection-to-Mission sections was drafted with assistance from Anthropic’s Claude; the authors specified the content, edited the text, and verified all technical claims, commands, and references. The con-duct software itself is developed with AI assistance, and with human review of all merged code. References con-duct. Center for Open Neuroscience. https://github.com/con/duct. The dev-side payoff (reaching back into outputs that would otherwise be gone) was an unexpected bonus. As LLM agents take on more of the executing (writing throwaway pipelines, exploring datasets, calling tools), the volume of unrecorded work explodes: more commands, more parallel streams, results produced faster than anyone reads them. RSEs are the people who decide whether that work remains auditable: who preserve the context, make it discoverable, and keep capture cheap enough that nobody skips the step. Integrating at the tool level saves each project from building its own monitoring and logging, and keeps the records uniform across tools, so the collection stays queryable as a whole.

items.abstract: Diagnosing production incidents is still largely manual: on-call engineers gather logs, errors and deployment history from separate tools before they can reason about a cause. Large language models (LLMs) can suggest root causes, but a model that sees only an incident summary lacks evidence, and an unchecked suggestion can mislead. This paper aims to give an LLM agent the evidence it needs while keeping a human in control. We present Phase 1 of an open, four-module platform: a non-blocking Java SDK that captures exceptions, latency and deployments; a multi-tenant Spring Boot backend that groups repeated errors into incidents by stack hash; a FastAPI service in which a tool-calling LLM investigates each incident only through audited APIs; and a dashboard where an operator approves or rejects every suggestion. We evaluate it by injecting seven kinds of real faults into an instrumented service. All 21 trials were detected, with mean detection times of 8–12 s for exception faults and 25–45 s for resource faults, and no incident was raised in 8 min of fault-free operation. The SDK added a median of 14 µs per captured error and stayed non-blocking when the backend was down. A successful investigation used about 11k–24k tokens and two to three minutes; of five graded suggestions, two were correct, two partly correct and one wrong despite a confidence of 0.78. The results show that telemetry-grounded investigation is practical for small teams, and that self-reported confidence must not replace human review.

items.title: Agentic artificial intelligence in mechanics of materials: A review of building tailored models on demand
items.abstract: Abstract In mechanics of materials, many powerful methods are accessible only to experts. Constitutive models, for example, describe the relation between stress and strain in materials and are a core ingredient of simulations from structural engineering to biomechanics. Yet building and using such models requires specialized expertise—a barrier for the many potential users trained in other fields. Artificial intelligence based on foundation models, increasingly organized as agents, is beginning to lower this barrier by allowing users to generate tailored models on demand. The same development is underway in many other fields where specialized tools have long been hand‐crafted anew for each task. We call this emerging paradigm the on‐the‐fly generation of physical models : from a plain request, an agent creates a physical model on demand—from scratch and tailored to the problem. Its appeal is accessibility and flexibility. As a consequence, the lasting artifact is no longer a fixed model but the orchestration and prompting of the agents that produce it. This review surveys the concepts behind the paradigm, within mechanics of materials and in neighboring fields, and examines them through two lenses: effectiveness (the accuracy of the generated models) and trustworthiness (their physical admissibility). Trustworthiness is pursued along two routes: deepening the agent's integration under explicit validation, or restraining its autonomy in favor of trusted components. Given the rapid progress of foundation models, and the bitter lesson that general methods leveraging computation tend to prevail, we call for paradigms designed to scale with this progress rather than to compete with it.

items.abstract: This paper mainly deals with the second order nonlinear difference equations with advanced argument where and is a ratio of odd positive integers. This paper presents an AI-based framework for the prediction and classification of oscillatory behavior in nonlinear discrete-time dynamical systems. The proposed approach employs artificial intelligence and machine learning techniques to analyze the dynamic behavior of nonlinear discrete-time systems and identify oscillatory and non-oscillatory solution patterns. Relevant system parameters and solution characteristics are extracted and used to develop predictive models capable of classifying the long-term behavior of system trajectories. The proposed framework provides an efficient data-driven approach for detecting oscillations and predicting the qualitative behavior of nonlinear discrete-time dynamical systems. items.abstract: On October 19th, 2026, a post on Substack https://open.substack.com/pub/generativevalue/p/what-has-to-go-right-to-justify-the?utm_source=share&utm_medium=android&r=3nsea2 asked a question that the AI industry has not answered: "What has to go right to justify thetrillions being spent on AI CapEx?" The post models $1.5 trillion in CapEx for 2027. It estimates the revenue threshold at $600 billion by late 2027 and $1.1 trillion by 2028. It names three conditions: the frontier keeps getting better at high-value work, AI diffuses through the economy, and value doesn't get whittled away by competition. The post is correct about the question. It is incomplete about the answer. This paper argues that the post names the cost of the stochastic architecture, but does not name the alternative architecture — one that requires almost no CapEx at all. The paper makes four claims: First: The stochastic path requires $1.5 trillion in CapEx. It cannot be certified under anyfunctional safety standard. It produces the four walls: CapEx, hallucination, energy, water, and AlCapone-LLM. Second: The deterministic path requires $2.1M–$6.5M for the first deployment. It can be certified under ISO 26262, IEC 61508, DO-178C, and IEC 62443. It runs on a $12microcontroller. Third: The ratio is roughly 1:500,000. The two paths are not competing on the same economics. Fourth: The 4 norms are the certification path. The deterministic architecture passes them byconstruction. The stochastic architecture cannot pass them at all. The paper does not argue that creativity needs scaling. It argues that creativity is selection.Selection requires a criterion. A criterion is not a scale. It is a discovery. The corpus has 300+papers to prove it.

items.title: AI and machine learning in healthcare: Diagnostics, decision support, and ethical governance in cross-border medical tourism
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) are rapidly evolving from experimental tools into integral components of clinical care. In diagnostics, treatment planning, and operational management, AI systems can augment clinicians&s; capabilities, enable earlier and more accurate interventions, and improve the patient experience—particularly for those seeking care across international borders. However, they also raise important questions about data privacy, algorithmic bias, transparency, and accountability. International organisations, notably the World Health Organization (WHO), now emphasise that AI in healthcare must be guided by robust ethical standards and tailored to the realities of diverse healthcare systems, including those that serve large numbers of medical tourists. This chapter examines how AI is being deployed throughout the medical tourism pathway—from early diagnosis and pre-travel screening to in-hospital decision support and post-travel follow-up—featuring real-world clinical examples and case studies from Apollo Hospitals in India and the Mayo Clinic in the United States. It also addresses the conditions under which AI can genuinely humanise, rather than dehumanise, globally mobile healthcare.

items.title: AI and Media: Challenges, Prospects and Opportunities
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is transforming the media ecosystem by changing how information is gathered, verified, produced, personalized, distributed and monetized. News organisations can use AI for transcription, translation, data analysis, recommendation, automated production, audience analytics, fact-checking support, visualisation and the creation of new formats. At the same time, AI introduces significant risks concerning misinformation, deepfakes, algorithmic bias, privacy, intellectual property, opacity, labour displacement, editorial accountability and the erosion of public trust. These tensions are particularly important in India, where the media environment is linguistically diverse, mobile-first, platform-dependent and characterised by a rapid expansion of digital and creator-led news. This conceptual paper examines the challenges, prospects and opportunities created by AI for Indian media and develops an integrated framework for responsible AI-enabled journalism. Drawing on stakeholder theory, the resource-based view, institutional theory, diffusion of innovations and the emerging literature on algorithmic and automated journalism, the paper conceptualises AI capability as an enabling resource whose value depends on editorial governance, human oversight, professional competence, data quality and regulatory conditions. The framework proposes that AI adoption influences media performance through a mediating mechanism of newsroom capability and workflow transformation, while ethical governance, organisational readiness and regulatory clarity moderate the relationship. The paper argues that AI should be treated neither as a substitute for journalism nor simply as a productivity tool, but as a socio-technical capability that must remain accountable to journalistic values. For Indian media, the most promising opportunities lie in multilingual journalism, accessibility, local and hyperlocal coverage, data-driven reporting, personalised public-interest information, newsroom efficiency and new digital business models. However, these opportunities can be realised only when media organisations establish transparent AI-use policies, verification protocols, disclosure standards, staff training, data safeguards and mechanisms for human editorial responsibility. The paper concludes with implications for media managers, journalists, educators, regulators and technology providers, and proposes directions for future empirical research.

items.title: AI and the reorganization of RSE work
items.abstract: Coding agents like Claude Code and GitHub Copilot have significant implications for the way software is built and maintained in the sciences. Some of these implications center around changes in practice, such as greater or worse productivity and the need for verification practices (He et al., 2025; O'Brien, 2025a; O’Brien, 2025b; Besser et al., 2026; O'Brien and Eisty, 2026). Another dimension of concern, however, is how research software development work will be reorganized around the presence of coding agents. Broader discourse has focused on the possibility of replacement or simple automation of software engineering work by agents, but, as with prior developments, the change is more likely to involve a more complex re-ordering of the work of producing software (Jarrahi, 2018; see also Gesing, 2025). Emerging work in industrial and open source contexts, for instance, suggests that coding agents can affect the interactions around code review (Song et al., 2024; Agarwal et al., 2026a), assume different roles in the development process (Agarwal et al., 2026b), and can change where particular kinds of development work fall in a team or community (Xu et al., 2025). This poster explores these shifts in the context of RSE work by examining dynamics of re-delegation going on around the adoption of coding agents by researchers and RSEs. Based on interviews with 25 RSEs and RSE managers in the US, we first outline these RSEs’ rationales about what makes research software development either amenable or unsuitable for the use of AI coding agents. These include niche codebases, siloed working environments, savvy end users, prevalence of prototyping, and the importance of problem formation. We then outline three dynamics of re-delegation, each of which represents a shift in the way work is divided up and assigned (or taken on) amongst human and non-human actors (Ribes et al., 2013). These are: enabling end-user development, delegating implementation, and taking on AI training roles. In some cases our interlocutors report quite different and sometimes contradictory experiences across these categories. This raises two questions that can help stimulate further discussion on this topic: 1) What aspects of RSE working environments might contribute to RSEs’ different experiences with AI coding agents? 2) What organizational changes could RSEs or RSE teams make that might mitigate some of the problems associated with the growing usage of AI coding agents while making best use of those agents’ benefits? items.title: AI as Co-Designer and Feedback Partner: Enhancing Human Judgment
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is shaping the future of higher education, tasking educators with transforming teaching, learning, and assessment practices to consider how AI can enhance the educational environment. With its increasing availability, it is important for administrators, faculty, and students to explore the practical nature of AI use prior to entry into the workforce. Faculty must also reevaluate how they approach assessing student learning, tasking them to rethink each assessment’s purpose, how it will inform future practice, and how it will prepare learners to use AI. Furthermore, faculty must also be prepared to consider the collaborative nature of AI, transforming their mindset to consider AI as an active co-designer and partner, one that does not seek to diminish the educator’s human judgment. This manuscript will articulate the importance of co-design, where AI and educators collaboratively shape assessment tools, and serve to champion feedback partnerships that enhance reflective practice for both students and faculty.

items.title: AI as intern, not oracle: a design logic for human–AI partnership in experiential entrepreneurship education
items.abstract: Abstract Entrepreneurship education (EE) is increasingly extending across disciplines and institutional contexts, creating pressure to sustain the facilitation, reflection and contextual responsiveness required by experiential learning. At the same time, the rapid adoption of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in higher education raises questions about how AI can support such experiential learning without assuming authority over the judgement and decision-making central to entrepreneurial action. This study develops and empirically examines an AI-as-intern design logic for experiential EE. Rather than positioning AI as an authoritative “oracle”, the framework establishes an intentionally asymmetric human-AI partnership. Here AI provides prompts, alternatives, provisional representations and process support, while learners and educators retain responsibility for contextual interpretation, evaluative judgement and consequential decisions. The study examines two postgraduate entrepreneurship cohorts at a UK university ( n = 60) using a custom AI-enabled platform integrated into normal teaching. Evidence comprised session recordings and transcripts, observational field notes, a post-workshop survey, and 12 semi-structured interviews. Findings show that students used AI primarily as process scaffolding and iterative support. Learners accepted, rejected, modified and combined AI-generated material, while team interaction created additional opportunities for scrutiny and contextual evaluation. Our findings do not establish improvements in students’ judgement, creativity or cognitive load, but do show how these activities remained active within a bounded human-AI arrangement. The paper contributes a pedagogic design logic for AI-enabled experiential EE and provides exploratory propositions for the design of human-AI pedagogy concerning human authority, evaluative judgement, collaborative oversight, creative sequencing and bounded scaffolding under conditions of scaling pressure.

items.title: AI Augmented Student Advising: A Comparative Study of LLMs and Advisor-Based Course Recommendations
items.abstract: Course placement in higher education is pivotal for student progression. Traditional advising can be effectively augmented by Large Language Models (LLMs) to ensure scalable guidance. Crucially, we propose a novel on-premises infrastructure that runs LLMs locally, ensuring strict student data privacy. We benchmarked four open-source LLMs against gold-standard responses from human advisors (n = 3) using 35 Information Systems student profiles, identifying GPT-OSS-120B as the optimal model. To guarantee real-world viability, we profiled the infrastructure's resource utilization across 112 sequentially processed cases. Additionally, we evaluated complex scenarios: undergraduate course substitutions (n = 10) and graduate prerequisite assessments (n = 10). Results indicate strong performance in substitutions but mixed outcomes for prerequisite assessments. We also determined the optimal model parameters for recommendation accuracy. To assess broader institutional utility, we expanded testing to include four additional disciplines: Marketing, Economics, Accounting, and Finance (n = 20 per major), demonstrating the system's potential for cross-disciplinary application. This study demonstrates that securely deployed, locally hosted LLMs can provide a privacy-compliant framework to assist academic advisors, though current performance highlights the necessity of continuous human oversight.

items.title: AI feedback does not motivate by itself: a motivational-meaning model for university physical education
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) can convert movement into scores, visual overlays, and corrective prompts, but technical precision does not determine how learners interpret that feedback. We develop a motivational-meaning model for university physical education (PE), integrating self-determination theory, feedback literacy, self-regulated learning, and motor-learning research. Its contribution is a context-specific account of how pedagogical framing, social visibility, and embodied verification organize the interpretation of an AI-feedback event. Informational and controlling meaning are distinguished from subsequent psychological-need experiences. Blocked translation denotes a temporary difficulty establishing a defensible basis for action, rather than a third motivational meaning. The model also proposes self-regulatory appropriation as the transfer of an externally supported feedback process into independent monitoring and adjustment; its distinctiveness from established self-regulation constructs remains an empirical question. Seven proposition groups specify separable predictions concerning framing, actionable information, contestability, evaluative exposure, discrepancy repair, skill transfer, and a secondary pathway to continued participation. The outcome structure distinguishes system engagement, acquisition performance, retention and transfer, affect and well-being, and voluntary physical activity. Continued participation is treated as a distal hypothesis requiring longitudinal evidence and attention to prior activity, health, habit, and opportunity. We outline independent measurement of event interpretation and need experience, tests that separate technical from perceived accuracy, and ethical, multilevel research designs. The model offers testable design principles rather than evidence that AI feedback improves learning or participation.

items.title: AI in smart cockpits: navigating compliance with the EU AI Act frameworks
items.abstract: The global smart cockpit market is undergoing explosive growth, with AI-enabled functionalities emerging as core components of modern vehicles. However, the integration of AI in smart cockpits has introduced complex compliance challenges under the EU AI Act and the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). This paper adopts a three-dimensional analytical framework (regulatory, technical, industrial practice) to systematically explore the compliance landscape, key dilemmas, and actionable solutions for smart cockpit AI systems. First, the paper clarifies the core obligations of high-risk and limited-risk AI systems under the EU regulatory framework. It also analyzes cross-regional regulatory conflicts among the EU, China, and the U.S., highlighting differences in data localization, consent mechanisms, and conformity assessment requirements. Second, the paper identifies risk-tier-specific compliance challenges, including data bias, transparency deficits, cross-border data transfer risks, as well as lifecycle management burdens. Additionally, it addresses emerging challenges brought by the integration of large language models (LLMs) in in-vehicle ecosystems, such as training data copyright verification and generative content controllability. Finally, the paper proposes an integrated compliance strategy. This strategy encompasses technical paths, full-lifecycle management, and cross-regional modular design to adapt to divergent regulatory requirements. The research provides a standardized compliance framework and practical tools for global automakers, helping balance technical innovation, user experience, and regulatory compliance to drive the sustainable development of the intelligent automotive industry.

items.title: AI Literacy among College Students and Its Influence on Academic Performance: A Study of Generative AI Tools
items.abstract: Abstract In today’s technology-driven world, Artificial Intelligence (AI) is becoming an important part of higher education. College students are increasingly using AI tools such as ChatGPT, Google Gemini, Microsoft Copilot, Claude, and Perplexity AI for their academic work. These tools help students prepare assignments and presentations, understand difficult topics, find ideas, improve their writing, and complete academic tasks in less time. However, simply knowing how to use AI is not enough. Students also need to understand whether the information provided by AI is correct, how to use it responsibly, and what problems may arise from depending too much on these tools. This study focuses on understanding the level of AI literacy among college students and its relationship with their academic performance. It will also study how familiar students are with generative AI tools, how often they use them, and for what academic purposes. The study will further examine the benefits students experience, the difficulties they face, and their understanding of issues such as academic honesty, originality, privacy, and responsible use of AI. The study will use a mixed-methods research design, combining both quantitative and qualitative methods. Quantitative information will be collected through a structured questionnaire using Google Forms. Interviews and open-ended questions will be used to understand students’ personal experiences, opinions, and attitudes towards AI in education. The study will include college students between 18 and 26 years of age from different academic backgrounds. The research will be limited to colleges in the Mumbai Metropolitan Region. The study is expected to provide a clear picture of how AI literacy is connected with students’ academic performance. The findings may also help colleges and teachers plan AI literacy programmes and create practical guidelines for the proper use of AI in education. Overall, the study aims to encourage students to use AI as a helpful learning tool while maintaining independent thinking, originality, and academic responsibility.

items.title: AI Safety as a Space between Fields
items.abstract: This chapter examines the novel task of making artificial intelligences safe through an analysis of 168 job postings from career platform https://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" xlink:href=" https://80000hours.org ">80000hours.org . Rather than viewing AI safety as a pre-paradigmatic field destined to solidify into clear professional boundaries, we analyse it as an interstitial network of expertise operating between academia, industry, government, and the non-profit sector. AI safety work, we find, takes place in a trading zone characterised by strategic ambiguity in organisational forms and domain expertise. This ambiguity stems from tensions built into the task itself: AI safety experts are expected to contribute to AI progress while attempting to control its risks, using dual-use methods that often advance both capabilities and oversight. These tensions shape hiring practices, with organisations seeking candidates who embody seemingly contradictory qualities – academic researchers and industry pragmatists, independent thinkers, and team players, highly specialised but effective communicators. We argue that such tensions are not temporary contentions to be resolved but rather constitute AI safety as a space between fields, attractive to multiple actors precisely because of its productive ambiguity.

items.title: Ai-Assisted Differentiated Instruction in Legal English: The Ailed Model
items.abstract: This article addresses one of the most important problems in the field of Legal English instruction: using artificial intelligence (AI) to organise effective, differentiated instruction for learners with diverse language skills. Legal English is a branch of English for Specific Purposes (ESP) that requires proficiency in legal terminology, legal genres, and legal discourse, as well as general language proficiency. Uniform instructional materials may be too challenging for some students and not challenging enough for others. The article proposes the AILED (AI-Assisted Legal English Differentiation) Model, which integrates AI-assisted differentiation of legal terminology, adaptation of instructional texts, and principles of differentiated instruction. The model has been developed after an in-depth review of literature on Legal English pedagogy, AI-assisted language learning, and differentiated instruction, as well as an analysis of placement-test data from 103 Master’s students enrolled in law and jurisprudence programmes at the International Scientific-Educational Center of the National Academy of Sciences of the Republic of Armenia. The placement data provide evidence of heterogeneous proficiency among law and jurisprudence students, supporting the need for differentiated Legal English instruction.

items.title: AI-Augmented Studio Pedagogy
items.abstract: The increasing integration of generative artificial intelligence (AI) into design practice has prompted product design education to reconsider the pedagogical foundations of studio-based learning. Although generative AI offers new opportunities for exploration, ideation, and design development, its unregulated use may undermine core designerly competencies, including reflective practice, material experimentation, and critical judgment. This article proposes an AI-augmented pedagogical framework that structures the integration of generative AI within the product design studio. Adopting a theoretically informed Research Through Design education approach, this study develops a pedagogical architecture articulated around four guiding principles, a five-phase studio model, and explicit regulatory mechanisms designed to support responsible AI use throughout the design process. The principal contribution of this article lies in the pedagogical operationalization of regulated co-intelligence. The proposed framework organizes interactions between students, teachers, peers, and generative AI systems in ways that preserve the foundations of designerly reasoning while fostering algorithmic reflexivity, critical AI literacy, and informed professional judgment. Designed as an adaptable pedagogical model, the framework provides a conceptual basis for future empirical research on the regulated integration of generative AI into studio-based design education.

items.title: AI-Based Fault Prediction for Small Solar PV Systems: An ESP32 Acquisition Unit and a Proposed Machine-Learning Framework
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) methods for photovoltaic (PV) fault diagnosis and prediction are usually developed on well-instrumented plants with reliable irradiance data and plentiful labelled examples, conditions that small, low-cost installations rarely meet. This paper presents a three-stage machine-learning framework for fault prediction in such installations, together with the ESP32-based acquisition unit that will supply its data. The unit is built and running. It measures PV voltage (GPIO34), current through an ACS712-20A sensor (GPIO35) and panel temperature through a DS18B20 sensor (GPIO4), computes power, and shows fixed-threshold status labels on a 16×2 I²C display. The AI framework is proposed and has not yet been implemented. Its first stage is an Isolation Forest trained only on normal-operation data, so that abnormal behaviour can be flagged before labelled fault data exist. Its second stage is a Random Forest classifier that assigns a fault class once staged-fault data have been collected. Its third stage predicts slowly developing faults: it fits trends to daily performance and thermal indices and estimates the number of days until each index crosses a fault threshold, giving an early warning before the fault becomes significant. Sudden faults such as open or short circuits cannot be predicted in this way and are only detected. items.title: AI-Driven Personalisation in Digital Payments: Examining Its Impact on Customer Trust
items.abstract: Abstract Digital India programme over a decade shown an upward performance by setting a benchmark. It is a flagship initiatives of the Government of India. It has digitally empowering the society and digital economy. Digital economy is an economic activities enhanced with the digital transformation using the digital computing tools. It provided various opportunities in the Banking and Fintech sectors. In current scenario Artificial Intelligence (AI) playing a very significant pivotal role by integrating the technology in all the sectors. It is enhancing the opportunities for the service provider and customer. Due to the rapid expansion of digital payment ecosystems, it has transformed the way how a consumers conduct their everyday financial transactions for purchasing their requirements either through online shopping i.e. e-commerce or visiting the store personal and using the digital banking or digital payment. In India, the digital payment especially using Unified Payments Interface (UPI) now has become a very important component of the digital financial ecosystem. Alongside this growth, the payment service providers are progressively integrating with the Artificial Intelligence (AI) technology to personalise their customer experiences. This is providing an enhance features through transaction recommendations to the customers with amazing discount features or offers in the payments using the digital payments. It further enables the customers in identifying their spending insights and intelligent alerts and adaptive customer support. This conceptual research proposes to examine the relationship between AI driven personalisation and customer trust in digital payment systems. The study propose to integrate from the perspectives of adopting the model Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology 2 (UTAUT2) with the trust theory. The proposed model considers AI personalisation, perceived usefulness, perceived relevance, transparency as among the key explanatory variables, with customer trust as the principal dependent construct. Behavioural intention and continuance intention are considered as potential outcomes of trust. The expected findings may provide very useful insight in the domain of digital banking, digital payment segment of the banks, fintech companies, and payment service providers to improve the trustworthy for the customer and responsible AI enabled payment ecosystems. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence, AI-driven personalisation, digital payments, UPI, customer trust.

items.title: AI-Driven Socratic Dialogues as Cognitive Scaffolds in Medical Scientific Writing
items.abstract: Medical students increasingly use large language models to generate manuscript text, bypassing the reasoning that scientific writing is meant to build. This monograph argues that the pedagogically defensible use of these tools is interrogative rather than generative. We map classical Socratic elements onto clinical writing tasks, compare the two architectures used to build Socratic writing tutors, describe how models are constrained to question rather than answer, and set out how to deploy such a coach in a medical curriculum. No study has yet tested this application directly; the supporting evidence is adjacent. A ready-to-use system prompt is supplied.

items.title: AI-Generated Deepfake Financial Scams: A Missing Liability Regime for Consumer Protection Frameworks
items.abstract: Abstract Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) outputs, such as deepfakes, can be useful for creating realistic simulations in education, news reporting, and the arts. However, the emergence of malicious deepfake scams has raised concerns about the quality and reliability of the information provided to social media users. This article argues that a liability regime for deepfakes is currently missing from consumer protection frameworks. Regulatory interventions do not explicitly target GenAI software developers and online social media platforms. However, the implementation of appropriate risk management safeguards is necessary to prevent unlawful deepfake activities. We contend that a shared liability regime for deepfakes among the multiple actors involved could offer adequate protection for victims of online financial fraud and would effectively target the deepfake supply chain. This shared liability regime would be complemented by the UK Financial Conduct Authority’s consumer duty rule, which acts as a preventive monitoring and enforcement mechanism to avoid foreseeable harm to consumers of AI applications.

items.title: AI-Powered Technologies in Foreign Language Education: Opportunities and Challenges
items.abstract: The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into foreign language education has initiated an unprecedented paradigm shift within higher education institutions worldwide. This expansive research paper explores the multifaceted impact of AI-powered technologies in the English as a Foreign Language (EFL) classroom, critically evaluating the dual concepts of revolutionary pedagogical opportunities and systemic instructional challenges. Utilizing a comprehensive mixed-methods research design incorporating a quantitative survey of 115 university students and qualitative, structured interviews with language faculty members, this study analyzes tools ranging from automated speech recognition (ASR) systems to advanced generative artificial intelligence and large language models (LLMs). The opportunities identified and expanded upon include augmented student engagement, ubiquitous exposure to immersive, authentic language environments, personalized feedback loops, and a significant reduction in foreign language speaking anxiety through non-judgmental digital interfaces. Conversely, the critical challenges encompass algorithmic biases, digital divide inequities, the structural degradation of independent academic writing skills, cognitive dependency, and the profound loss of socio-pragmatic and cultural context in text generation. Ultimately, the paper argues that a balanced, hybrid pedagogical framework underpinned by proactive digital literacy is required to responsibly navigate these emerging dynamics, ensuring that artificial intelligence acts as a cognitive amplifier rather than a replacement for human-centered communicative interaction.
