items.title: AI‐Driven Onboard Detection of Ocean Eddies by Haishao‐1 Spaceborne SAR
items.abstract: Onboard processing for remote sensing satellites has long been of interest in ocean monitoring because it can provide timely information on rapidly changing ocean environments. Recently, the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into onboard processing has emerged as an active research topic. However, application scenarios and on-orbit demonstrations of AI-based onboard processing remain limited. In this study, we achieved the first on-orbit detection of ocean eddies using AI on the Haishao-1 (HS-1) spaceborne synthetic aperture radar (SAR) satellite, marking the first attempt to monitor an ocean dynamic process directly onboard. Specifically, an onboard application module was developed for HS-1, integrating image preprocessing and deep learning-based detection based on our previously developed Eddy Detection based on YOLO (EOLO) model. On-orbit experiments verified stable execution of the application module. Ground reproduction of the tasks using hardware identical to the onboard computing units yielded an average processing time of 3.4-6.1 s per image. Evaluation against expert annotations of 288 HS-1 scenes showed that EOLO, originally developed using Sentinel-1 imagery, achieved an F1 score of 78% after threshold adjustment. The application module has also been deployed on the Haishao-2 platform for Arctic sea ice extraction, further demonstrating its extensibility. This study presents the implementation and on-orbit validation of the onboard application module, providing a practical reference for future applications.

items.title: Algorithmic Management, Employee Voice, and Procedural Justice: A Governance Framework for Accountable AI-Assisted Organizations
items.abstract: Algorithmic systems increasingly allocate tasks, rank performance, flag anomalies, and recommend decisions that affect employment conditions. This critical integrative review examines how algorithmic management may reshape employee voice and perceptions of procedural justice in AI-assisted organizations. It distinguishes automated recommendations from fully automated decisions, information disclosure from effective contestability, and worker participation from symbolic consultation. Established research on algorithmic control, organizational justice, algorithmic transparency, and human-AI decision structures provides the conceptual basis. The article develops an accountability chain linking data provenance, decision rights, reviewability, employee explanation, correction pathways, and evaluation of organizational outcomes. It argues that the mere presence of a human reviewer does not demonstrate meaningful oversight; review authority, adequate information, and the ability to change an outcome are separate requirements. Potential benefits of automation include consistency and early detection of harmful errors, while risks include opaque sanctions, strategic data manipulation, and the displacement of responsibility. No primary interviews, experimental observations, or quantitative effect estimates are reported. The proposed empirical agenda combines process tracing, employee surveys, decision-log audits, scenario-based experiments, and organizational comparisons. The framework can be supported only if its specified safeguards improve measurable fairness, accuracy, employee trust, and organizational performance beyond existing governance practices. algorithmic management; employee voice; procedural justice; AI governance; human oversight; organizational accountability

items.title: AllPath: Layered Verification for a Deployed, Self-Revising LLM Trading Agent under Human-Gated and Autonomous Regimes
items.abstract: LLM trading agents are evaluated almost exclusively in backtests and autonomous benchmark harnesses. Deployment, where actions are irreversible, raises a different question: who verifies the agent's actions, and which failures can each verifier structurally catch? We report on AllPath, a personal LLM trading agent deployed against a live paper-brokerage account. The system watches positions through a deterministic rules engine, and each night it reviews its own day and proposes revisions to its own trading strategies. Verification is split across three layers. Code verifies what must not depend on judgment: deterministic gates enforce risk limits and block any strategy revision that fails an integrity check. The agent verifies itself within fixed bounds: its nightly review has an iteration cap and no tools that can act. A human verifies judgment, through approval screens that show the current state of each proposal. We also compared two verification policies for the agent's self-revisions on the live system: two and a half weeks with every self-revision human-gated, then five weeks with reflection revisions auto-applied behind the same code gates, while the operator's chat channel stayed human-gated throughout. Each layer caught a different kind of failure. The code gates rejected no proposal; their role was keeping revisions consistent. The human rejected two proposals that passed every code check, both over a disagreement about the market, and later removed 11 of the 19 rules the agent had added on its own, at a median lag of eight days. The most instructive production incidents, such as strategies silently left unmonitored, passed every gate; the operator found them by hand, and the fix each time was an interface change that makes the condition visible. We contribute the layered architecture, the two-regime account, and a production incident taxonomy, none observable in a backtest.

items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is making a swift impact on the processes of teaching and learning by influencing lesson development, student assessment methods, and teachers’ perceptions of their profession. However, existing literature primarily focuses on the technical aspects of AI technologies rather than examining how secondary school teachers actually use these technologies when preparing lessons. The purpose of this study is to explore the experiences of secondary school teachers in using AI technologies in their teaching practices. Purposive sampling will be employed to select 15–20 teachers working with students in Grades 9–12 who have been using AI technologies for at least one semester. Data will be collected through semi-structured interviews and analyzed using content analysis. The findings are expected to provide a detailed understanding of teachers’ perceptions of AI integration into their professional practices, its influence on teaching and learning processes, the challenges and benefits they encounter, and the extent to which the use of AI tools shapes their professional identities.

items.title: An empirical study on how social engineering and persuasion principles training affects senior citizens’ responses to SMiShing attacks
items.abstract: Purpose The purpose of this research study was set to address the problem of cyberattacks, such as phishing delivered via short message service (SMS) or SMiShing, targeted towards senior citizens. In 2023, they lost over $36m to such attacks. Phishing success increases when attackers use persuasion principles that bypass logical decision-making and rely on heuristics. Security education, training, and awareness (SETA) programs can reduce susceptibility, yet little research investigated SETA programs that incorporate these principles. Design/methodology/approach This research was conducted in three phases, beginning with Subject Matter Experts’ evaluation of SMiShing messages operationalizing these persuasion principles for use in this study’s instrument. The next phase was a pilot study. The third phase was the main data collection and analysis phase. This research employed a pretest-posttest design to evaluate the efficacy of its novel SETA program. The SETA program used Behavioral Skills Training methodology with 118 senior citizens from South Florida and Central Massachusetts. Findings The experimental results indicated a statistically significant mean difference between pretest and posttest group scores (F = 6.604, df = 5, p = 0.011) in identifying SMiShing messages that operationalize the principles of persuasion used in social engineering. Specifically, the pretest group’s mean score was 73.62, and the posttest group’s mean score was 79.28. The calculated effect size (η2 = 0.054) nears the threshold for a medium effect (η2 = 0.06). Practical implications Recognizing persuasion in SMiShing messages helped senior citizens better detect these cyberattacks. Practical implications include incorporating persuasion principles into the SETA framework to address evolving cyberattacks (e.g. deepfakes, vishing) that are being enhanced by generative artificial intelligence. Social implications As a group, senior citizens have lost millions to cyberattacks. SETA programs that incorporate principles of persuasion appear to help reduce the financial losses this group incurs from cyberattacks and may also improve senior citizens’ confidence and reduce fear when using communication technology. Originality/value This research’s original contribution is the integration of persuasion principles into cybersecurity training programs, helping senior citizens quickly recognize the malicious intent of SMiShing messages, which apply psychological pressures to achieve the attacker’s goals.

items.title: Anatomy of Off-Policy Policy Gradient: Importance Sampling, KL Regularization, and Baselines
items.abstract: Reinforcement learning has become a central tool for large language model (LLM) post-training, where policy gradient methods are routinely deployed off-policy, even though vanilla policy gradient assumes on-policy sampling. We study when such off-policy deployment is justified, and what roles its core ingredients, including importance sampling, KL regularization, and baselines, play in handling the resulting distribution shift. We show that for a general class of off-policy policy gradient updates, consistency, in the sense that the optimal policy remains a stationary point, requires one of two structures at the optimal policy: trajectory-level importance weighting, which suffers from the well-known curse of horizon, or KL regularization with a baseline equal to the optimal soft value, instantiated by the grouped mean. Focusing on the KL route, we identify it with the group-relative policy gradient (GRPG) update, establish an equivalence to a trajectory-level Bellman residual minimization objective, and obtain a finite-sample regret bound under all-policy coverage. This also gives a theoretical account of a variant of the empirically successful GRPO objective. We further uncover a hidden role of baselines in the off-policy setting: a constant shift in the baseline implements pessimism, the standard remedy in offline RL for partial data coverage. We instantiate this via the asymmetric REINFORCE objective, and connect it to the game-theoretic offline RL framework, showing a regret bound with single-policy coverage. Together, these results offer a unified theoretical view of off-policy policy gradient in LLM post-training and connect it to classical ideas in offline RL.
